title: Newfoundland preserves large fossils about 560 million years old
body: At Mistaken Point, on Newfoundland's coast, rocks dating from roughly 580 to 560 million years ago preserve large organisms from the Ediacaran Period. The rocks formed under deep marine conditions.
takeaway: The fossils record large life appearing after an immense span of Earth's history dominated by microbes.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Mistaken Point (2016)
visual: fern-like Ediacaran fossils in a slab of coastal rock

title: One coast preserves a coal-age forest and its neighbours
body: The Joggins cliffs in Nova Scotia contain fossils from about 318 to 303 million years ago. Layers preserve traces of an estuarine bay, a floodplain rainforest and a fire-prone plain with freshwater pools.
takeaway: Fossils can show how habitats were arranged near each other, rather than merely which species lived at the time.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Joggins Fossil Cliffs (2008)
visual: a fossil tree trunk embedded upright in layered coastal cliffs

title: A deep-sea shrimp can release a cloud of light
body: NOAA has documented the deep-sea shrimp Heterocarpus ensifer emitting luminous material from glands near its mouth. A chemical reaction produces the light in the surrounding water.
takeaway: Bioluminescence can move away from an animal, unlike colouring that stays on its body.
source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, What Is Bioluminescence?
visual: a deep-sea shrimp releasing a small glowing cloud into dark water

title: The candela measures light in a way that accounts for human vision
body: The candela measures brightness in a particular direction. Its international definition uses light at 540 terahertz, in the green part of the spectrum where the eye is highly sensitive in bright conditions.
takeaway: Two lights with the same physical power can seem to have different brightness if their colours differ.
source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, Candela
